notes.text: Thou shalt take — This seems to be required of each master of a family, either upon his first settlement, or once every year at one of their three feasts, when they were obliged to go up to Jerusalem.

A Syrian — So Jacob was, partly by his original, as being born of Syrian parents, as were Abraham and Rebecca, both of Chaldea or Mesopotamia, which was a part of Syria largely so called, partly by his education and conversation; and partly by his relations, his wives being such, and his children too by their mother's. Ready to perish - Either through want and poverty; (See Gen. xxviii, 11, 20; xxxii, 10,) or through the rage of his brother Esau, and the treachery of his father-in-law Laban.
It — The basket of first-fruits, ver. 2.

Thou shalt rejoice — Thou shalt hereby enabled to take comfort in all thy employments, when thou hast sanctified them by giving God his portion. It is the will of God, that we should be chearful not only in our attendance upon his holy ordinances, but in our enjoyment of the gifts of his providence. Whatever good thing God gives us, we should make the most comfortable use of it we can, still tracing the streams to the fountain of all consolation.

glossa.text: *And when thou shalt have entered,* etc. Just as the Israelites in the land of promise are bidden to offer their first-fruits for a giving of thanks, because they were snatched out of Egypt, so let us, entering through the spiritual Jordan — that is, baptism — into the land of the Church, place in the basket of our manner of life the first-fruits of good working, and let us offer them to God upon the altar of the catholic faith, that our priest Christ may receive them; and there let us confess to the Lord, saying that the Syrian — who is interpreted "lofty," or "moistening," that is, the devil — was pursuing our father, that is, the first-formed man, that, having deceived him through pride, gluttony and avarice, he might deprive him of the possession of paradise; whence as an exile he sojourned in the Egypt of this world in a small number, because many followed idolatry, and few remained faithful. But after the law was given and more arose, receiving the knowledge and the faith of the one God, the Egyptians — that is, the demons — afflicted them, laying upon them the most grievous burdens of sins. But God looked upon the affliction and the labour of the human race, and sent his Son, who is called his hand and his arm, that he might snatch them out of the power of darkness and carry them over into the kingdom of light. So he handed over to us a land flowing with milk and honey, that is, the mighty Church, where there is the milk of innocence and the honeycomb of doctrine, whereby little ones are nourished, and the honey of a sweet and manifold wisdom, whereby the perfect are filled.

*Which the Lord thy God hath given,* etc. As if to say, I offer nothing but what he has given; for every good thing is from God.

*Of the Lord thy God.* Who will keep them as it were beneath his eyes, and will render them on that day, a just judge.

*Thou shalt feast,* with a spiritual banquet, of which it is said: *Eat, O friends, and be inebriated, my dearly beloved ((Cantic. V))*.

*And the Levite,* the true minister of God, taken from among men and appointed for men in the things that pertain to God.

notes.text: He — He that makes God his habitation and refuge.
Bear thee — Sustain or uphold thee in thy goings, as we do a child.

The lion — Shall lie prostrate at thy feet, and thou shalt securely put thy feet upon his neck. Dragon - By which he understands all pernicious creatures, though never so strong, and all sorts of enemies.

Because — This and the two following verses are the words of God. God is praised for his works, ver. 1-5. The doom of the wicked, from the eternal God, ver. 6-9. The prosperity of the righteous, ver. 10-15. A psalm or song for the sabbath-day.

glossa.text:
*The praise of a canticle.* Praise is human also: but this praise is of a canticle, because it is nothing if not divine. For this psalm is a hymn against the demons. The Prophet therefore says of any holy man whatsoever: *He that dwelleth in the help,* etc.

((CASS.)) He shows that the temptations of the devil were overcome through humility by Christ, and by his own, who remain in the help of God, that we too through him may learn to overcome temptations, because he is the door through which *jauna*, if any man shall enter in, he shall go in, and shall go out, and pasture shall come forth.

((AUG.)) Christ is the door; to enter through him is to imitate him, not in godhead, and power, and miracles, but in that wherein he was made for us, that is, in the humility to which he calls, saying: *Learn of me, because I am meek and humble of heart.* Out of this psalm the devil tempted Christ. But Christ's temptation is our teaching, and following him we overcome by him.

*He that dwelleth.* ((CASS.)) He describes first the man who trusts in God alone, wholly walled about by the protection of God. *He that dwelleth,* that is, who sets all his hope always not in himself, but in God, shall be protected by God in every way. Note the correspondence of the words: for as he always *dwelleth,* so also shall he always *abide.* The one he affirms, namely that he *dwelleth;* the other he promises, namely that he *shall be protected.*

*He shall abide in the protection of the God of heaven.* That is to say, that he turn not aside to the right hand or to the left, as in the Old Testament it was commanded to the children of Israel, that they should walk by the king's highway, not turning aside to the right hand or to the left. The king's highway is the way of Christ our king, who so ran the way of the world that he was neither enticed by prosperity, nor broken by adversity.

*My God.* ((CASS.)) Lest thou think that after the upholding and the refuge nothing further is to be asked for, he adds: *In him will I trust,* lest at any time he presume of himself; and if Adam had done this, he would have stood well.

*For thou art.* ((AUG.)) One Christ is head and body, of whom he speaks now as of the head, now as of the body, the person not being changed. Therefore diligently mark where he treats of Christ according to the head, and where according to the members. *The Most High.* In the height is the refuge of God, deep in secret, that flight may be made from the wrath to come. For many so make for themselves the refuge of God, whereby they flee from temporal evils. *Thou hast made the Most High thy refuge,* that is, by rising again, by ascending, thou hast made the refuge high, that I may now hope to follow *speram* whither thou hast gone before.
((ID.)) *The tabernacle of God* is the flesh, etc., *as far as* this is rightly taken of Christ.

*For to his angels.* This the tempter said to the Lord, when he tempted him: this he cast up against him, doubting of his Godhead. But Christ was tempted for our sake, that in him also we might learn to overcome the tempter.

((AUG.)) So also he willed to be baptized by a servant, not for his own need, but for man's profit, that we should not disdain to be baptized by our fellow servants.
*In their hands they shall bear thee up.* ((ID.)) By the hands of angels Christ was lifted up into heaven, etc., *as far as* he who cannot be overcome.

*Upon the asp.* After the human infirmity, the divine power is shown, which commands such creatures. And he treats of Christ according to the members. *And he shall trample.* ((AUG.)) The Church, which is wary of his cunning, treads upon the serpent. *The lion.* He rages openly against the martyrs.

The dragon lies in wait through the heretics, that he may corrupt the virgin of Christ, whence the Apostle: *I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you a chaste virgin to Christ ((II Cor. XI))*.

*Because he hoped in me.* ((AUG.)) Thirdly, the words of God, by which he consoles the Church, to which he promises both defence here, and rewards in the world to come. ((CASS.)) He gives charge to the angels concerning thee, saying: *Because in me.* The certainty of the promise, through the promise of God.
*He shall cry to me.* ((AUG.)) There is no need to fear in tribulation, etc., *as far as* at that time let us labour the more to resist.

notes.text: But what saith he — Moses. Even these words, so remarkably applicable to the subject before us. All is done ready to thy hand. The word is nigh thee - Within thy reach; easy to be understood, remembered, practiced. This is eminently true of the word of faith - The gospel. Which we preach - The sum of which is, If thy heart believe in Christ, and thy life confess him, thou shalt be saved.
If thou confess with thy mouth — Even in time of persecution, when such a confession may send thee to the lions.

For with the heart — Not the understanding only. Man believeth to righteousness - So as to obtain justification. And with the mouth confession is made - So as to obtain final salvation. Confession here implies the whole of outward, as believing does the root of all inward, religion.
Isaiah xxviii, 16.

The same Lord of all is rich — So that his blessings are never to be exhausted, nor is he ever constrained to hold his hand. The great truth proposed in ver. 11 is so repeated here, and in ver. 13, and farther confirmed, ver. 14, 15, as not only to imply, that "whosoever calleth upon him shall be saved;" but also that the will of God is, that all should savingly call upon him.
Joel ii, 32.

glossa.text:
*The word is nigh.* That is, it is useful, or there is nothing unfitting either to say or to believe. Or *nigh,* because it is not far from the nature of minds: and by the manner of speaking, that which is said to us that we may believe.

*This is the word. ((AUG., Tract. 80, in Joannem.))* Of which the Lord says: *For you are clean by reason of the word which I have spoken to you,* etc. *as far as* for in the word itself one thing is the sound that passes, another the power that remains.

*That if thou confess. ((AUG.))* Behold the praise of faith and its reward. The praise of faith is, if thou shalt have believed that Jesus is Lord, etc., *as far as* who goes before it in a resurrection suited to itself, that is, in justification.

*With the heart we believe.* Other things a man can do unwilling, but he cannot believe save willing.

*Confession. ((AUG., in Psal. XXX, concione III.))* To confess is to say what is in the heart, etc., *as far as* because he so believes, so also he ought in the mouth, that he may so preach.

*Who call upon him.* He that prays calls upon; but this assuredly he cannot do, unless he first believe. They therefore who call upon him not only believe, but also pray, so that after anyone's mind has believed it may not cease to ask that which God promised to them that watch with the whole heart, because to believe gives the remission of sins. But to call upon obtains the promises of God.

notes.text: The wilderness — Supposed by some to have been in Judea; by others to have been that great desert of Horeb or Sinai, where the children of Israel were tried for forty years, and Moses and Elijah fasted forty days. Matt. iv, 1; Mark i, 12.
Deut. viii, 3.

I give it to whomsoever I will — Not so, Satan. It is God, not thou, that putteth down one, and setteth up another: although sometimes Satan, by God's permission, may occasion great revolutions in the world.
Deut. vi, 13.
Psalm xci, 11.
Deut. vi, 16.
A convenient season — In the garden of Gethsemane, chap. xxii, 53.

glossa.text:
*And he was led. ((AMBR.))* He was led into the desert with this purpose, that he might provoke the devil; for unless that one had contended, this one would not have conquered for me; with this mystery, that he might free Adam from exile; with this example, that he might show us that the devil envies those who reach out toward better things.

*Into the desert.* Historically: into that desert which is between Jerusalem and Jericho, where he had figuratively said that Adam had been overcome by the devil.
*He was hungry. ((BEDA.))* It is not written of Moses or of Elias, etc., *as far as* but he hungers not so much for the food of the body as for the salvation of the soul.

*If thou be the Son of God. ((AMBR.))* He had known that the Son of God would come, but he did not think that he had come through the weakness of the body, etc., *as far as* he who is not fed with this word does not live.

*It is written.* He teaches that one must fight rather with doctrine than with miracles, with humility rather than with power, and that nothing is to be done at the devil's pleasure, nor out of any regard for displaying his power.

*And he brought him.* Luke follows the thing as it was done, setting avarice in the middle and pride last, according to the manners of the present time, because pride rages after all the virtues. Matthew does not follow the order of the history, but that of the temptations of Adam.

*To thee will I give.* He says these things out of arrogance, not because the whole world is his, for there are some good men. *It is delivered to me.* Power is not from the devil, but it is nevertheless exposed to the snares of the devil. Nor is the ordering of the powers evil on that account, because the powers are exposed to evil.
*Thou therefore. ((BEDA.))* The devil, saying to the Saviour: *If falling down thou wilt adore me,* hears in return that he himself ought rather to adore him, his Lord and his God.

*If thou be the Son of God.* In all the temptations he does this, that he may learn whether he be the Son of God. But Christ so tempers his answer as to leave it in doubt: *Cast thyself down.* Him whom neither gluttony nor avarice overcame, vainglory tempts, in case perhaps the very boasting of his own victory might avail to cast him down. *Cast.* This word befits him who busies himself to hurl all men headlong. In which he is shown to be weak, since he can harm no one unless that one has first cast himself down.

*It is written.* Because he had put forward an example from the Scriptures, he is overcome by examples from the Scriptures. But the devil uses the testimonies of the Scriptures through the heretics, not to teach, but to deceive.

*To the angels. ((BEDA.))* This prophecy is not of Christ, but of a holy man. And even if it were of Christ, he ought also to have remembered what follows: *Thou shalt walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and thou shalt trample under foot the lion and the dragon ((Psal. XC))*. But of the help of the angels he speaks as though to one who is weak; of his own treading down he keeps silence, like a shuffler.
*And being ended. ((ID.))* The three temptations being overcome, he says that every temptation was ended, etc., *as far as* yet he dreads to press on, lest he be more often triumphed over.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: You shall therefore keep my statutes and my ordinances; which if a man does, he shall live in them. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: Formula-cited: 'Moses writes about the righteousness of the law' introduces 'The one who does them will live by them' — a near-verbatim quotation of Leviticus 18:5 ('which if a man do, he shall live in them'). Paul makes it the voice of law-righteousness over against faith-righteousness. Also quoted at Galatians 3:12; high recurrence in Paul.

echoes.text: It is not in heaven, that you should say, “Who will go up for us to heaven, and bring it to us, and proclaim it to us, that we may do it?” Neither is it beyond the sea, that you should say, “Who will go over the sea for us, and bring it to us, and proclaim it to us, that we may do it?” But the word is very near to you, in your mouth and in your heart, that you may do it.
echoes.note: Formula-introduced ('the righteousness of faith says'): 'Do not say in your heart, Who will ascend into heaven... Who will descend into the abyss... The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart' — a sustained verbatim quotation of Deuteronomy 30:12-14, reworked christologically (ascend = bring Christ down; descend into the abyss = bring Christ up from the dead). High volume, the structural backbone of the pericope.

echoes.text: Don’t say in your heart, after Yahweh your God has thrust them out from before you, saying, “For my righteousness Yahweh has brought me in to possess this land”; because Yahweh drives them out before you because of the wickedness of these nations.
echoes.note: The opening 'Do not say in your heart' in 10:6 conflates Deuteronomy 30:12 with the warning formula of Deuteronomy 9:4 ('Do not say in your heart... my righteousness'), which directly concerns self-righteousness. Strong verbal borrowing that splices the anti-self-righteousness warning onto the faith-word quotation. Widely recognized double allusion.

echoes.text: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh, “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious cornerstone of a sure foundation. He who believes shall not act hastily.
echoes.note: Formula-cited: 'the Scripture says, Whoever believes in him will not be put to shame/disappointed' — a quotation of Isaiah 28:16 (the precious cornerstone in Zion). Paul adds the universalizing 'whoever' (pas). Recurs at Romans 9:33, knitting chapters 9-10 together; high volume and recurrence.

echoes.text: It will happen that whoever will call on Yahweh’s name shall be saved; for in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be those who escape, as Yahweh has said, and among the remnant, those whom Yahweh calls.
echoes.note: Formula-cited climax: 'Whoever will call on the name of the Lord will be saved' — verbatim quotation of Joel 2:32 (LXX 3:5). Paul reads kyrios as the risen Jesus (10:9, 'Jesus is Lord'), grounding the Jew-Greek universalism of 10:12. Also cited in Acts 2:21; high recurrence.

echoes.text: For this commandment which I command you this day is not too hard for you or too distant.
echoes.note: The immediately preceding verse — 'this commandment is not too hard for you, nor is it far off' — sets up the not-in-heaven/not-beyond-the-sea contrast Paul exploits. Borrowed context for the 'word is near' argument even though only vv.12-14 are quoted.

echoes.text: But the word is very near to you, in your mouth and in your heart, that you may do it.
echoes.note: The 'mouth... heart' pairing of the Deut quotation is redeployed by Paul in 10:9-10 (confess with the mouth, believe in the heart). This is an exegetical extension of the quoted text — Paul mines the very words 'mouth/heart' to structure confession and faith. Strong internal echo of the source just cited.

echoes.text: They mount up to the sky; they go down again to the depths. Their soul melts away because of trouble.
echoes.note: 'They mount up to heaven, they go down to the depths (abyss)' — the heaven/abyss merism for cosmic extremity. Paul's pairing 'ascend into heaven / descend into the abyss' may draw on this stock idiom; Deut 30 itself says 'beyond the sea,' so the 'abyss' wording suggests a secondary scriptural idiom. Disputed.

echoes.text: You will know that I am in the midst of Israel, and that I am Yahweh, your God, and there is no one else; and my people will never again be disappointed.
echoes.note: 'You shall... not be put to shame' in Joel 2:27, just before the quoted v.32, shares the not-ashamed motif Paul draws from Isaiah 28:16. Possible reinforcing echo from the Joel context Paul is already mining. Disputed.

echoes.text: The earth was formless and empty. Darkness was on the surface of the deep and God’s Spirit was hovering over the surface of the waters.
echoes.note: 'the abyss' (abyssos) as primeval deep; Paul's substitution of 'abyss' for Deut's 'beyond the sea' carries cosmic/death overtones (= realm of the dead, whence Christ is raised). Faint scriptural background for the abyss imagery. Disputed.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: You shall remember all the way which Yahweh your God has led you these forty years in the wilderness, that he might humble you, to prove you, to know what was in your heart, whether you would keep his commandments, or not. He humbled you, and allowed you to be hungry, and fed you with manna, which you didn’t know, neither did your fathers know; that he might teach you that man does not live by bread only, but man lives by every word that proceeds out of […]
echoes.note: Jesus' reply 'Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word of God' quotes Deuteronomy 8:3 (LXX). The forty days of fasting and testing in the wilderness deliberately recapitulate Israel's forty years where God humbled them with hunger and fed them manna 'that he might teach you that man does not live by bread alone.' Maximal Volume and Coherence: the whole temptation is framed as a re-run of Israel's wilderness test.

echoes.text: You shall fear Yahweh your God; and you shall serve him, and shall swear by his name.
echoes.note: 'You shall worship the Lord your God, and you shall serve him only' renders Deuteronomy 6:13 (LXX, which adds 'worship/proskyneo' and 'only/mono'). High Volume verbatim citation; the Shema context (Deut 6) anchors the second/third temptation answers in Israel's covenant loyalty.

echoes.text: You shall not tempt Yahweh your God, as you tempted him in Massah.
echoes.note: 'You shall not tempt the Lord your God' quotes Deuteronomy 6:16 (LXX), which itself recalls Israel's testing of God at Massah (Exod 17:1-7). Verbatim citation answering the pinnacle temptation; strong Recurrence with the other Deuteronomy quotations in the pericope.

echoes.text: For he will put his angels in charge of you, to guard you in all your ways. They will bear you up in their hands, so that you won’t dash your foot against a stone.
echoes.note: The devil quotes 'He will put his angels in charge of you... on their hands they will bear you up, lest you dash your foot against a stone' from Psalm 91:11-12 (LXX 90). High Volume verbatim citation, placed in Satan's mouth as a misuse of Scripture; the Deuteronomy reply rebuts it.

echoes.text: He was there with Yahweh forty days and forty nights; he neither ate bread, nor drank water. He wrote on the tablets the words of the covenant, the ten commandments.
echoes.note: The forty-day fast echoes Moses on Sinai, forty days and nights without bread or water (Exod 34:28; cf. Deut 9:9). Coherence with Jesus as new Moses/Israel; Availability strong, though the dominant frame is Israel's forty years rather than Moses' forty days.

echoes.text: He arose, and ate and drank, and went in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights to Horeb the Mount of God.
echoes.note: Elijah's forty-day fast journey to Horeb is a secondary candidate for the forty-day motif. Lower Volume than the Exodus/Deuteronomy frame, but Luke's special interest in Elijah later in this very chapter (vv.25-26) raises its Coherence.

echoes.text: Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which Yahweh God had made. He said to the woman, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden?’” The woman said to the serpent, “We may eat fruit from the trees of the garden, but not the fruit of the tree which is in the middle of the garden. God has said, ‘You shall not eat of it, neither shall you touch it, lest you die.’” The serpent said to the woman, “You won’t surely […]
echoes.note: Jesus tested over food by the tempter/serpent inverts Adam and Eve's failure under the same kind of test; figural Adam-Christ logic latent in Luke's genealogy ending at Adam (3:38) immediately before. Faint Volume but coherent within Luke's structure.

echoes.text: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: The devil's offer of 'all the kingdoms of the world... all this authority and their glory' contrasts with the authority, glory, and kingdom rightly given to the one like a son of man in Daniel 7:14. Contested and faint; the irony works only if the Danielic gift of dominion is in view.
